readerTitle: Two founders: one started with a product, one started with a complaint
caseNote: 가상 사례 (기업 교육 서비스, 심야 음식점, 근무 교대 앱) + 실제 연구 (CB Insights 스타트업 실패 원인 분석)를 일반적으로 인용
insight: 아이디어를 평가할 때는 내가 만들 것이 얼마나 좋은지가 아니라, 누가 어떤 문제 때문에 이미 돈과 시간을 쓰고 있는지를 먼저 본다.
misconception: 좋은 제품을 잘 만들면 고객은 따라온다. 완성도와 전문성이 성공을 결정한다.

sources.text: CB Insights, The Top Reasons Startups Fail (스타트업 사후 분석 보고서, 2014년 이후 여러 차례 갱신)
Dana, Sam, 근무 교대 앱 사례는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: CB Insights 보고서에서 'no market need'가 가장 많이 꼽힌 실패 원인 중 하나라는 점을 게시 전 최신 보고서로 확인하세요. 버전마다 순위와 비율(2014년 약 42%, 이후 개정판에서는 다른 수치)이 달라 카드에는 구체적 수치를 쓰지 않고 'among the most cited reasons'로만 적었습니다.
Dana와 Sam 사례, 간호사 20명 인터뷰, 밤 11시·새벽 3시 배달 등은 모두 설명용 가상 설정입니다. 실제 기업처럼 보이지 않도록 이미지에 상호나 로고를 넣지 않습니다.

cards.title: Two founders: one started with a product, one started with a complaint
body: Dana and Sam both started businesses the same spring.
Dana had a polished product ready to sell. Sam had a problem he kept hearing about. A year later, only one of them had steady customers.

image.label: Two founders side by side: one holding a finished product, one listening to people
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 화면 왼쪽에는 반짝이는 완성품 상자(교육 교재와 슬라이드)를 든 여성 창업자, 오른쪽에는 메모장을 들고 병원 유니폼 차림의 사람들 이야기를 듣는 남성 요리사. 실제 상표나 로고는 넣지 않음.

cards.title: Who is more likely to have paying customers in a year?
body: **Dana**, an experienced HR trainer, builds a six-week leadership course for small companies. Slides, workbook and website are all ready on day one.

**Sam**, a cook, lives near a hospital. Night-shift nurses keep telling him only vending machines are open after 10 pm. Before cooking anything, he asks 20 nurses what they eat now and what they would pay for a hot meal.

options.text: Dana. She has a finished, professional product and deep expertise
options.feedback: Polish and skill are real assets. But no customer has yet said they feel the problem her course solves, so she is betting that it exists.

options.text: Sam. He started from a problem people already feel every shift
options.feedback: He knows who hurts, when, and what they do today. His offer can be rough at first because the need is already there.

options.text: Too early to tell. It depends on who markets better
options.feedback: Marketing matters, but it amplifies demand that already exists. It rarely creates a need people don't feel.

cards.title: Dana heard "looks great." Sam heard "when can I order?"
body: Company owners praised Dana's course, then didn't book it. Leadership training felt nice to have, not urgent. Months later she learned their real headache: getting new hires useful in their first two weeks.

Sam started small. Four dishes, delivered to the hospital entrance at 11 pm and 3 am, ordered through a group chat. Within weeks he was selling out. His food wasn't fancy. It solved a problem people faced every night.

image.label: Empty training room on one side, a line of nurses at a late-night food counter on the other
image.brief: 화면을 반으로 나눔. 왼쪽은 의자가 비어 있는 교육장과 화이트보드, 오른쪽은 밤하늘 아래 병원 입구 앞 작은 음식 카운터에 간호사들이 줄 선 장면. 따뜻한 조명은 오른쪽에만. 병원 이름, 로고 없음.

cards.title: Problem before solution
body: **Problem before solution** means you first understand a specific problem: who has it, how often, and how much it costs them. Only then do you decide what to build or sell.
Dana fell in love with her answer and went looking for someone with the matching question. Sam fell in love with the question. His answer could change. The problem kept him pointed at real customers.

image.label: Arrow from 'Problem' to 'Solution', with the reverse arrow crossed out
image.brief: 간단한 인포그래픽. 왼쪽 'Problem' 상자에서 오른쪽 'Solution' 상자로 굵은 화살표. 그 아래 반대 방향 화살표(Solution → looking for a problem)는 회색 점선에 X 표시.

cards.title: Four questions that test a problem.
body: Before you build, try to answer these without mentioning your product:
list: **Who** exactly has it? Not "small businesses", but "owners of 10-person firms hiring their first managers"
**How often** does it happen? Every night beats once a year
**What do they do today?** Vending machines, spreadsheets, a nephew who helps out
**What does that cost them?** Time, money, stress, lost customers
cards.callout: A workaround is the strongest clue. If people already spend money or effort on a bad fix, the problem is real.

cards.title: Good work, wrong problem.
body: Research firm CB Insights has reviewed hundreds of startup post-mortems. "No market need" keeps showing up among the most cited reasons for failure. Many of those teams built something well. Too few people had the problem it solved.
The same happens inside companies. A team spends a quarter on a report or a new process nobody asked for, while the complaint everyone repeats in meetings goes unfixed.

cards.title: Problem first doesn't mean customers design it.
body: Customers know their pain well. They are often poor at inventing the fix. Listen for the problem, then design the answer yourself.
Don't research forever, either. A few dozen conversations and one small, cheap test usually tell you enough.
And sometimes a new tool comes first. That's fine, as long as you then go find people with a real problem it solves, before you build more.

cards.title: Now it's a software idea.
body: A developer wants to build an app that lets restaurant staff swap shifts. She has a few months of savings and wants to start well.

options.text: Build a full version with swaps, chat and payroll export, then show it to managers
options.feedback: She'd get a polished product fast, but months of work would rest on a guess about what managers actually struggle with.

options.text: Interview 15 restaurant managers about how shift swaps work today and what goes wrong
options.feedback: It costs a few weeks, not months. She learns whether swaps really hurt, what workaround they use, and what it costs them.

options.text: Post an online survey: "Would you use an app to swap shifts?"
options.feedback: Quick and cheap, but it asks people to judge her solution, not describe their problem. "Sure, maybe" tells her little.

cards.title: Fall in love with the problem, not your solution.
body: A well-made product for a problem nobody feels still won't sell. Start with who hurts, how often, and what they do about it today.
**Try it today:** write your idea's problem in one sentence without naming your product. Then list what those people do about it right now.
